# ============================================================================
# PRODUCTION-READY TRACKING CONFIGURATION
# ============================================================================

class ProductionTrackingConfig:
    """
    Production-ready configuration for query execution tracking.
    """
    
    @staticmethod
    def get_spark_session_with_tracking(app_name: str, 
                                       log_dir: str = "/tmp/spark-events",
                                       enable_ui: bool = True) -> SparkSession:
        """
        Create a Spark session with comprehensive tracking enabled.
        
        Args:
            app_name: Application name
            log_dir: Directory for event logs
            enable_ui: Whether to enable Spark UI
            
        Returns:
            Configured SparkSession
        """
        builder = SparkSession.builder \
            .appName(app_name) \
            .config("spark.eventLog.enabled", "true") \
            .config("spark.eventLog.dir", log_dir) \
            .config("spark.ui.enabled", str(enable_ui).lower()) \
            .config("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "true") \
            .config("spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled", "true") \
            .config("spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled", "true") \
            .config("spark.sql.adaptive.localShuffleReader.enabled", "true") \
            .config("spark.sql.statistics.histogram.enabled", "true") \
            .config("spark.sql.cbo.enabled", "true") \
            .config("spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold", "10485760") \
            .config("spark.executor.metrics.pollingInterval", "1000ms") \
            .config("spark.metrics.appStatusSource.enabled", "true")
        
        return builder.getOrCreate()
    
    @staticmethod
    def get_tracking_recommendations() -> Dict[str, str]:
        """Get recommended tracking configurations."""
        return {
            "spark.eventLog.enabled": "true - Enable event logging for history server",
            "spark.eventLog.dir": "/path/to/logs - Directory for event logs",
            "spark.sql.adaptive.enabled": "true - Enable adaptive query execution",
            "spark.ui.enabled": "true - Enable Spark UI for monitoring",
            "spark.executor.metrics.pollingInterval": "1000ms - Metrics collection frequency",
            "spark.sql.statistics.histogram.enabled": "true - Enable histogram statistics",
            "spark.sql.cbo.enabled": "true - Enable cost-based optimizer",
            "spark.metrics.namespace": "app_name - Namespace for metrics"
        }


# ============================================================================
# COMPREHENSIVE EXAMPLE WITH ALL PATTERNS
# ============================================================================

def comprehensive_tracking_example():
    """
    Comprehensive example demonstrating all tracking patterns together.
    """
    
    # Initialize Spark with tracking configuration
    spark = ProductionTrackingConfig.get_spark_session_with_tracking(
        "Comprehensive Tracking Example"
    )
    
    spark.sparkContext.setLogLevel("WARN")
    
    print("\n" + "="*80)
    print("COMPREHENSIVE TRACKING EXAMPLE")
    print("="*80 + "\n")
    
    # Create sample datasets
    print("Creating sample datasets...")
    
    # Large sales dataset
    sales_data = []
    for i in range(1, 5001):
        sales_data.append((
            i,
            f"2024-{(i % 12) + 1:02d}-{(i % 28) + 1:02d}",
            f"Product_{i % 50}",
            f"Category_{i % 10}",
            round(10 + (i * 3.7) % 1000, 2),
            f"Store_{i % 100}",
            f"Region_{i % 5}"
        ))
    
    sales_schema = StructType([
        StructField("sale_id", IntegerType(), False),
        StructField("sale_date", StringType(), False),
        StructField("product", StringType(), False),
        StructField("category", StringType(), False),
        StructField("amount", DoubleType(), False),
        StructField("store", StringType(), False),
        StructField("region", StringType(), False)
    ])
    
    sales_df = spark.createDataFrame(sales_data, sales_schema)
    
    # Product dimension
    product_data = [(f"Product_{i}", f"Category_{i % 10}", 
                    f"Brand_{i % 20}", round(5 + i * 2.5, 2)) 
                   for i in range(50)]
    
    product_schema = StructType([
        StructField("product", StringType(), False),
        StructField("category", StringType(), False),
        StructField("brand", StringType(), False),
        StructField("cost", DoubleType(), False)
    ])
    
    product_df = spark.createDataFrame(product_data, product_schema)
    
    print(f"Sales dataset: {sales_df.count():,} records")
    print(f"Product dataset: {product_df.count():,} records\n")
    
    # Initialize all trackers
    integrated_tracker = IntegratedExecutionTracker(spark)
    perf_tracker = PerformanceOptimizationTracker(spark)
    batch_tracker = BatchQueryTracker(spark)
    
    # Define multiple queries for batch tracking
    print("Setting up batch queries...")
    
    # Query 1: Daily sales summary
    daily_summary = sales_df.groupBy("sale_date", "region").agg(
        sum("amount").alias("daily_sales"),
        count("*").alias("num_transactions"),
        avg("amount").alias("avg_transaction")
    ).orderBy("sale_date")
    
    batch_tracker.add_query("Daily Sales Summary", daily_summary)
    
    # Query 2: Category performance
    category_perf = sales_df.groupBy("category").agg(
        sum("amount").alias("total_sales"),
        count("*").alias("transactions"),
        avg("amount").alias("avg_sale"),
        max("amount").alias("max_sale"),
        min("amount").alias("min_sale")
    ).orderBy(desc("total_sales"))
    
    batch_tracker.add_query("Category Performance", category_perf)
    
    # Query 3: Product profitability with join
    product_profit = sales_df.join(product_df, "product").select(
        col("product"),
        col("category"),
        col("brand"),
        col("amount"),
        col("cost"),
        (col("amount") - col("cost")).alias("profit")
    ).groupBy("brand", "category").agg(
        sum("profit").alias("total_profit"),
        sum("amount").alias("total_revenue"),
        count("*").alias("num_sales")
    ).orderBy(desc("total_profit"))
    
    batch_tracker.add_query("Product Profitability Analysis", product_profit)
    
    # Query 4: Regional trends
    regional_trends = sales_df.groupBy("region", "category").agg(
        sum("amount").alias("regional_sales"),
        count("*").alias("transactions")
    ).withColumn(
        "avg_transaction",
        col("regional_sales") / col("transactions")
    ).orderBy("region", desc("regional_sales"))
    
    batch_tracker.add_query("Regional Trends", regional_trends)
    
    # Execute batch
    print("\nExecuting batch queries with comprehensive tracking...")
    batch_results = batch_tracker.execute_batch()
    
    # Detailed analysis of one query
    print("\n" + "="*80)
    print("DETAILED ANALYSIS: Product Profitability")
    print("="*80 + "\n")
    
    # Track with all patterns
    result_df, comprehensive_report = integrated_tracker.track_comprehensive(
        product_profit,
        "Detailed Product Profitability Analysis"
    )
    
    # Performance analysis
    perf_analysis = perf_tracker.analyze_performance(
        product_profit,
        "Product Profitability Query"
    )
    
    # Show results
    print("\nQuery Results (Top 10):")
    result_df.show(10)
    
    # Export batch report
    batch_report = batch_tracker.get_batch_report()
    
    print("\n" + "="*80)
    print("BATCH EXECUTION COMPLETE")
    print("="*80)
    
    print(f"\nBatch ID: {batch_report['batch_id']}")
    print(f"Total Queries: {batch_report['total_queries']}")
    
    # Final recommendations
    print("\n" + "="*80)
    print("OPTIMIZATION RECOMMENDATIONS")
    print("="*80 + "\n")
    
    all_recommendations = []
    for analysis in perf_tracker.get_all_analyses():
        all_recommendations.extend(analysis['recommendations'])
    
    if all_recommendations:
        print("Based on performance analysis, consider the following:")
        for i, rec in enumerate(all_recommendations, 1):
            print(f"\n{i}. [{rec['severity']}] {rec['type']}")
            print(f"   {rec['message']}")
    else:
        print("No optimization recommendations - performance is optimal!")
    
    print("\n" + "="*80)
    print("COMPREHENSIVE EXAMPLE COMPLETE")
    print("="*80 + "\n")
    
    # Cleanup
    spark.stop()

class TrackingPatternTests:
    """
    Test suite for tracking patterns.
    """
    
    @staticmethod
    def test_query_id_tracking():
        """Test Query ID Tracking Pattern."""
        print("\nTesting Query ID Tracking Pattern...")
        
        spark = SparkSession.builder \
            .appName("Test Query ID Tracking") \
            .master("local[*]") \
            .getOrCreate()
        
        tracker = QueryIDTracker(spark)
        
        # Create test data
        test_df = spark.range(100).selectExpr("id", "id * 2 as value")
        
        # Test tracking
        result_df, info = tracker.execute_with_tracking(
            "Test Query",
            lambda: test_df.groupBy().sum("value")
        )
        
        assert info['status'] == 'SUCCESS', "Query should succeed"
        assert info['record_count'] > 0, "Should have records"
        assert 'query_id' in info, "Should have query ID"
        
        print("✓ Query ID Tracking test passed")
        spark.stop()
    
    @staticmethod
    def test_dag_tracking():
        """Test Execution DAG Pattern."""
        print("\nTesting Execution DAG Pattern...")
        
        spark = SparkSession.builder \
            .appName("Test DAG Tracking") \
            .master("local[*]") \
            .getOrCreate()
        
        tracker = ExecutionDAGTracker(spark)
        
        # Create test data
        test_df = spark.range(100).selectExpr("id", "id % 10 as group")
        agg_df = test_df.groupBy("group").count()
        
        # Test DAG capture
        dag_info = tracker.capture_dag(agg_df, "Test DAG")
        
        assert 'dag_id' in dag_info, "Should have DAG ID"
        assert 'physical_plan' in dag_info, "Should have physical plan"
        assert dag_info['num_partitions'] > 0, "Should have partitions"
        
        print("✓ DAG Tracking test passed")
        spark.stop()
    
    @staticmethod
    def test_timeline_tracking():
        """Test Execution Timeline Pattern."""
        print("\nTesting Execution Timeline Pattern...")
        
        spark = SparkSession.builder \
            .appName("Test Timeline Tracking") \
            .master("local[*]") \
            .getOrCreate()
        
        tracker = ExecutionTimelineTracker(spark)
        
        # Create test data
        test_df = spark.range(100).selectExpr("id", "id * 2 as value")
        
        # Test timeline tracking
        timeline = tracker.track_timeline(test_df, "Test Timeline", execute=True)
        
        assert 'timeline_id' in timeline, "Should have timeline ID"
        assert len(timeline['events']) > 0, "Should have events"
        assert 'total_duration' in timeline, "Should have total duration"
        
        print("✓ Timeline Tracking test passed")
        spark.stop()
    
    @staticmethod
    def run_all_tests():
        """Run all tracking pattern tests."""
        print("\n" + "="*80)
        print("RUNNING TRACKING PATTERN TESTS")
        print("="*80)
        
        try:
            TrackingPatternTests.test_query_id_tracking()
            TrackingPatternTests.test_dag_tracking()
            TrackingPatternTests.test_timeline_tracking()
            
            print("\n" + "="*80)
            print("ALL TESTS PASSED ✓")
            print("="*80 + "\n")
            
        except AssertionError as e:
            print(f"\n✗ Test failed: {str(e)}\n")
            raise
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"\n✗ Unexpected error: {str(e)}\n")
            raise

BEST PRACTICES:
===============

1. Always enable event logging in production:
   spark.conf.set("spark.eventLog.enabled", "true")

2. Use appropriate tracking level based on needs:
   - Development: Comprehensive tracking
   - Testing: Stage and timeline tracking
   - Production: Query ID and performance tracking

3. Set meaningful query names for easier debugging

4. Export tracking data for historical analysis

5. Monitor skew and shuffle metrics regularly

6. Use batch tracking for comparing multiple approaches

7. Implement alerting based on performance thresholds

8. Regularly review and act on optimization recommendations

9. Keep tracking data for trend analysis

10. Document query patterns and their performance characteristics


TROUBLESHOOTING:
================

Common Issues and Solutions:

1. High Skew Ratio:
   Problem: Data is unevenly distributed across partitions
   Solution: Use salting, custom partitioning, or AQE skew join optimization
   
2. Excessive Shuffles:
   Problem: Too many data movements across network
   Solution: Optimize join order, use broadcast joins, reduce aggregations
   
3. Low Throughput:
   Problem: Processing too few records per second
   Solution: Increase parallelism, optimize partition size, check for bottlenecks
   
4. Memory Issues:
   Problem: Out of memory errors during tracking
   Solution: Reduce tracking granularity, increase executor memory
   
5. Long Execution Times:
   Problem: Queries taking too long to complete
   Solution: Review DAG, optimize plan, check for data skew


PERFORMANCE METRICS REFERENCE:
===============================

Key Metrics to Monitor:

1. Execution Time: Total time from query submission to completion
2. Record Count: Number of records processed
3. Partition Count: Number of data partitions
4. Skew Ratio: Max partition size / Avg partition size (ideal: < 2.0)
5. Shuffle Count: Number of shuffle operations (minimize)
6. Stage Count: Number of execution stages
7. Task Count: Total number of tasks
8. Records/Second: Throughput metric
9. Memory Usage: Memory consumed during execution
10. Spill Metrics: Data spilled to disk (should be minimal)


INTEGRATION WITH MONITORING TOOLS:

1. Prometheus Integration:

4. Multi-Query Optimization:
   Optimize multiple related queries together

5. Resource-Aware Tracking:
   Consider cluster resources in recommendations


LIMITATIONS AND CONSIDERATIONS:
================================

1. Overhead: Tracking adds some overhead to execution
   - Minimal for query-level tracking
   - Higher for task-level tracking

2. Storage: Event logs can consume significant disk space
   - Implement log rotation
   - Archive old logs

3. Network: Metrics collection may increase network traffic
   - Use sampling for high-frequency metrics
   - Aggregate before transmission

4. Complexity: Comprehensive tracking adds code complexity
   - Use selectively based on needs
   - Document tracking strategy

# Method 1: Using stack() function (most efficient)

).select("product", "quarter_data.quarter", "quarter_data.sales")

# Method 3: Dynamic unpivot for unknown columns
def unpivot_dynamic(df, id_vars, value_vars, var_name="variable", value_name="value"):
    """
    Dynamic unpivot function that works with any set of columns
    
    Args:
        df: Input DataFrame
        id_vars: List of identifier columns to keep
        value_vars: List of columns to unpivot
        var_name: Name for the variable column
        value_name: Name for the value column
    """
    # Create stack expression
    stack_expr = f"stack({len(value_vars)}"
    for var in value_vars:
        stack_expr += f", '{var}', `{var}`"
    stack_expr += f") as ({var_name}, {value_name})"
    
    # Select id columns and unpivoted columns
    return df.selectExpr(*id_vars, stack_expr)

# Use dynamic unpivot
value_columns = ["Q1_sales", "Q2_sales", "Q3_sales", "Q4_sales"]
long_df_dynamic = unpivot_dynamic(
    wide_df, 
    id_vars=["product"], 
    value_vars=value_columns,
    var_name="quarter",
    value_name="sales"
)

# Recursive hierarchy flattening (using iterative joins)
def flatten_hierarchy(df, max_depth=10):
    """
    Flatten hierarchical structure by creating path columns
    """
    result = df.select(
        "employee_id",
        "title",
        "manager_id",
        "level",
        col("employee_id").alias("path_id"),
        col("title").alias("path_title")
    )
    
    for i in range(1, max_depth):
        result = result.alias("curr") \
            .join(
                df.alias(f"parent_{i}"),
                col("curr.manager_id") == col(f"parent_{i}.employee_id"),
                "left"
            ) \
            .select(
                col("curr.employee_id"),
                col("curr.title"),
                col("curr.manager_id"),
                col("curr.level"),
                concat_ws(" > ", 
                    coalesce(col(f"parent_{i}.title"), lit("")),
                    col("curr.path_title")
                ).alias("path_title"),
                col("curr.path_id")
            )
        
        # Break if no more parents found
        if result.filter(col("manager_id").isNotNull()).count() == 0:
            break
    
    return result

flattened_hierarchy = flatten_hierarchy(org_df)

# UTILITY FUNCTIONS FOR RESHAPING
# ============================================================================
print("\n" + "="*80)
print("UTILITY FUNCTIONS FOR DATA RESHAPING")
print("="*80)

def generic_unpivot(df, id_cols, value_cols, var_name="variable", value_name="value"):
    """
    Generic unpivot function for wide-to-long transformation
    
    Args:
        df: Input DataFrame
        id_cols: List of identifier columns
        value_cols: List of columns to unpivot
        var_name: Name for variable column
        value_name: Name for value column
    
    Returns:
        Unpivoted DataFrame
    """
    stack_expr = f"stack({len(value_cols)}, "
    stack_expr += ", ".join([f"'{col}', `{col}`" for col in value_cols])
    stack_expr += f") as (`{var_name}`, `{value_name}`)"
    
    return df.selectExpr(*[f"`{col}`" for col in id_cols], stack_expr)

def generic_pivot(df, index_col, pivot_col, value_col, agg_func="first"):
    """
    Generic pivot function for long-to-wide transformation
    
    Args:
        df: Input DataFrame
        index_col: Column to use as index
        pivot_col: Column to pivot
        value_col: Column containing values
        agg_func: Aggregation function to use
    
    Returns:
        Pivoted DataFrame
    """
    if agg_func == "first":
        return df.groupBy(index_col).pivot(pivot_col).agg(first(value_col))
    elif agg_func == "sum":
        return df.groupBy(index_col).pivot(pivot_col).agg(_sum(value_col))
    elif agg_func == "avg":
        return df.groupBy(index_col).pivot(pivot_col).agg(avg(value_col))
    elif agg_func == "count":
        return df.groupBy(index_col).pivot(pivot_col).agg(count(value_col))
    else:
        return df.groupBy(index_col).pivot(pivot_col).agg(first(value_col))

def flatten_struct_columns(df, separator="_"):
    """
    Flatten all struct columns in a DataFrame
    
    Args:
        df: Input DataFrame
        separator: Separator for nested column names
    
    Returns:
        DataFrame with flattened struct columns
    """
    flat_cols = []
    nested_cols = []
    
    for field in df.schema.fields:
        if isinstance(field.dataType, StructType):
            nested_cols.append(field.name)
            for nested_field in field.dataType.fields:
                flat_cols.append(
                    col(f"{field.name}.{nested_field.name}")
                    .alias(f"{field.name}{separator}{nested_field.name}")
                )
        else:
            flat_cols.append(col(field.name))
    
    return df.select(flat_cols)

def explode_array_columns(df):
    """
    Explode all array columns in a DataFrame
    
    Args:
        df: Input DataFrame
    
    Returns:
        DataFrame with exploded array columns
    """
    array_cols = [field.name for field in df.schema.fields 
                  if isinstance(field.dataType, ArrayType)]
    
    result_df = df
    for array_col in array_cols:
        result_df = result_df.withColumn(
            f"{array_col}_exploded",
            explode(col(array_col))
        )
    
    return result_df

# Scenario 1: Time-series reshaping (lag/lead transformations)
print("\n--- Scenario 1: Time-Series Reshaping ---")

from pyspark.sql.window import Window

ts_data = [
    ("Product_A", "2024-01-01", 100),
    ("Product_A", "2024-01-02", 120),
    ("Product_A", "2024-01-03", 110),
    ("Product_B", "2024-01-01", 80),
    ("Product_B", "2024-01-02", 90),
    ("Product_B", "2024-01-03", 85)
]

ts_df = spark.createDataFrame(ts_data, ["product", "date", "sales"])

print("\nOriginal Time-Series Data:")
ts_df.show()

# Create lagged columns (wide format with temporal context)
window_spec = Window.partitionBy("product").orderBy("date")

ts_wide = ts_df.withColumn("sales_prev_1", F.lag("sales", 1).over(window_spec)) \
    .withColumn("sales_prev_2", F.lag("sales", 2).over(window_spec)) \
    .withColumn("sales_next_1", F.lead("sales", 1).over(window_spec)) \
    .withColumn("sales_change", col("sales") - F.lag("sales", 1).over(window_spec))

print("\nTime-Series with Lag/Lead (Wide Format):")
ts_wide.show()

# Convert back to long format for analysis
ts_long = ts_wide.selectExpr(
    "product",
    "date",
    "stack(5, " +
    "'current', sales, " +
    "'prev_1', sales_prev_1, " +
    "'prev_2', sales_prev_2, " +
    "'next_1', sales_next_1, " +
    "'change', sales_change" +
    ") as (metric_type, metric_value)"
).filter(col("metric_value").isNotNull())

print("\nTime-Series Metrics in Long Format:")
ts_long.show()

]

ecommerce_raw_df = spark.createDataFrame(

     "products", "prices", "quantities", "categories"]

print("\nStep 1: Raw E-Commerce Data (Denormalized):")

# Step 2: Normalize into separate tables
print("\nStep 2: Normalize into Relational Tables")

# Customer dimension (would typically have more attributes)
customer_dim = ecommerce_raw_df.select("customer_id").distinct() \
    .withColumn("customer_key", F.monotonically_increasing_id())

print("\nCustomer Dimension:")
customer_dim.show()

# Order header
order_header = ecommerce_raw_df.select(
    "order_id",
    "customer_id",
    col("timestamp").cast("timestamp").alias("order_timestamp")
).distinct()

print("\nOrder Header:")
order_header.show()

# Order line items (normalized)
order_lines = ecommerce_raw_df.select(
    "order_id",
    explode(
        F.arrays_zip(
            split(col("products"), "\\|"),
            split(col("prices"), "\\|"),
            split(col("quantities"), "\\|"),
            split(col("categories"), "\\|")
        )
    ).alias("item")
).select(
    "order_id",
    col("item.0").alias("product_name"),
    col("item.1").cast("int").alias("price"),
    col("item.2").cast("int").alias("quantity"),
    col("item.3").alias("category")
).withColumn("line_item_id", F.monotonically_increasing_id())

print("\nOrder Line Items (Normalized):")
order_lines.show()

# Step 3: Create analytical denormalized view
print("\nStep 3: Create Analytical Denormalized View")

analytical_view = order_header \
    .join(order_lines, "order_id") \
    .withColumn("line_total", col("price") * col("quantity")) \
    .select(
        "order_id",
        "customer_id",
        "order_timestamp",
        "product_name",
        "category",
        "price",
        "quantity",
        "line_total"
    )

print("\nAnalytical Denormalized View:")
analytical_view.show()

# Step 4: Create aggregated summary (wide format)
print("\nStep 4: Create Summary Reports")

# Summary by category (pivot)
category_summary = analytical_view.groupBy("order_id", "customer_id") \
    .pivot("category") \
    .agg(_sum("line_total").alias("total"))

print("\nCategory Summary (Pivoted):")
category_summary.show()

# Customer purchase summary with nested structure
customer_summary = analytical_view.groupBy("customer_id") \
    .agg(
        count("order_id").alias("total_orders"),
        _sum("line_total").alias("total_revenue"),
        collect_list(
            struct(
                "order_id",
                "order_timestamp",
                "product_name",
                "category",
                "line_total"
            )
        ).alias("purchase_history")
    )

print("\nCustomer Summary with Nested Purchase History:")
customer_summary.show(truncate=False)
customer_summary.printSchema()

def safe_pivot(df, group_col, pivot_col, value_col, pivot_values=None):
    """
    Safe pivot with validation and error handling
    """
    try:
        # Validate columns exist
        required_cols = [group_col, pivot_col, value_col]
        missing_cols = [c for c in required_cols if c not in df.columns]
        
        if missing_cols:
            raise ValueError(f"Missing columns: {missing_cols}")
        
        # Check for nulls in key columns
        null_counts = df.select(
            [_sum(when(col(c).isNull(), 1).otherwise(0)).alias(c) 
             for c in [group_col, pivot_col]]
        ).collect()[0].asDict()
        
        if any(null_counts.values()):
            print(f"Warning: Null values found in key columns: {null_counts}")
        
        # Perform pivot
        if pivot_values:
            result = df.groupBy(group_col).pivot(pivot_col, pivot_values).agg(first(value_col))
        else:
            result = df.groupBy(group_col).pivot(pivot_col).agg(first(value_col))
        
        # Validate result
        result_count = result.count()
        expected_count = df.select(group_col).distinct().count()
        
        if result_count != expected_count:
            print(f"Warning: Row count mismatch. Expected: {expected_count}, Got: {result_count}")
        
        return result
        
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Error during pivot: {str(e)}")
        raise

def validate_reshape(original_df, reshaped_df, id_cols, value_cols):
    """
    Validate that reshaping preserved data integrity
    """
    print("\n--- Data Integrity Validation ---")
    
    # Check row counts
    original_count = original_df.count()
    reshaped_count = reshaped_df.count()
    print(f"Original rows: {original_count}")
    print(f"Reshaped rows: {reshaped_count}")
    
    # Check for duplicates
    id_count = reshaped_df.select(id_cols).distinct().count()
    if id_count != reshaped_count:
        print(f"Warning: Duplicates detected! Unique IDs: {id_count}, Total rows: {reshaped_count}")
    
    # Check for nulls
    null_counts = reshaped_df.select(
        [_sum(when(col(c).isNull(), 1).otherwise(0)).alias(c) 
         for c in value_cols]
    ).collect()[0].asDict()
    
    if any(null_counts.values()):
        print(f"Null values in reshaped data: {null_counts}")
    
    # Check value preservation (sum of values should match)
    for val_col in value_cols:
        if val_col in original_df.columns:
            original_sum = original_df.select(_sum(col(val_col))).collect()[0][0]
            reshaped_sum = reshaped_df.select(_sum(col(val_col))).collect()[0][0]
            
            if original_sum != reshaped_sum:
                print(f"Warning: Sum mismatch for {val_col}. Original: {original_sum}, Reshaped: {reshaped_sum}")
            else:
                print(f"✓ Sum validated for {val_col}: {original_sum}")

def create_surrogate_key(df, key_columns, key_name="surrogate_key"):
    """
    Create a surrogate key based on natural keys with hash for consistency
    
    Args:
        df: Input DataFrame
        key_columns: List of columns to use for creating surrogate key
        key_name: Name of the surrogate key column
    
    Returns:
        DataFrame with surrogate key
    """
    from pyspark.sql.functions import md5, concat_ws, row_number
    
    # Create hash-based surrogate key
    df_with_key = df.withColumn(
        key_name,
        md5(concat_ws("||", *[col(c) for c in key_columns]))
    )
    
    return df_with_key

def detect_pivot_cardinality(df, pivot_column, threshold=1000):
    """
    Check if pivot operation is safe based on cardinality
    
    Args:
        df: Input DataFrame
        pivot_column: Column to pivot on
        threshold: Maximum safe cardinality
    
    Returns:
        Boolean indicating if pivot is safe
    """
    cardinality = df.select(pivot_column).distinct().count()
    
    print(f"\nPivot Cardinality Check:")
    print(f"Column: {pivot_column}")
    print(f"Distinct values: {cardinality}")
    print(f"Threshold: {threshold}")
    
    if cardinality > threshold:
        print(f"⚠ WARNING: High cardinality ({cardinality}). Pivot may be slow or fail.")
        print(f"Consider filtering data or using alternative approach.")
        return False
    else:
        print(f"✓ Safe to pivot ({cardinality} columns will be created)")
        return True

def smart_unpivot(df, id_cols, exclude_cols=None):
    """
    Automatically unpivot all non-ID columns
    
    Args:
        df: Input DataFrame
        id_cols: List of identifier columns to preserve
        exclude_cols: List of columns to exclude from unpivoting
    
    Returns:
        Unpivoted DataFrame
    """
    exclude_cols = exclude_cols or []
    all_exclude = set(id_cols + exclude_cols)
    
    # Get columns to unpivot
    value_cols = [c for c in df.columns if c not in all_exclude]
    
    print(f"\nSmart Unpivot:")
    print(f"ID columns: {id_cols}")
    print(f"Value columns: {value_cols}")
    
    # Create stack expression
    stack_expr = f"stack({len(value_cols)}, "
    stack_expr += ", ".join([f"'{col}', `{col}`" for col in value_cols])
    stack_expr += ") as (attribute, value)"
    
    return df.selectExpr(*[f"`{c}`" for c in id_cols], stack_expr)

def conditional_aggregate(df, group_cols, agg_col, conditions):
    """
    Create conditional aggregations (similar to CASE WHEN in SQL)
    
    Args:
        df: Input DataFrame
        group_cols: Columns to group by
        agg_col: Column to aggregate
        conditions: Dict of {condition_name: condition_expression}
    
    Returns:
        DataFrame with conditional aggregations
    """
    agg_exprs = []
    
    for name, condition in conditions.items():
        agg_exprs.append(
            _sum(when(condition, col(agg_col)).otherwise(0)).alias(name)
        )
    
    return df.groupBy(group_cols).agg(*agg_exprs)

# SCD Type 2 - Track historical changes with effective dates
print("\n--- SCD Type 2 Implementation ---")

# Current dimension data
current_dimension = spark.createDataFrame([
    (1, "Product_A", "Category_1", "2024-01-01", "9999-12-31", True),
    (2, "Product_B", "Category_2", "2024-01-01", "9999-12-31", True),
    (3, "Product_C", "Category_1", "2024-01-01", "9999-12-31", True)
], ["product_key", "product_name", "category", "effective_date", "end_date", "is_current"])

print("\nCurrent Dimension:")
current_dimension.show()

# New incoming data with changes
incoming_data = spark.createDataFrame([
    ("Product_A", "Category_1"),  # No change
    ("Product_B", "Category_3"),  # Category changed
    ("Product_D", "Category_2")   # New product
], ["product_name", "category"])

print("\nIncoming Data:")
incoming_data.show()

# Identify changes
from pyspark.sql.functions import current_date

changes = incoming_data.alias("new") \
    .join(
        current_dimension.filter(col("is_current") == True).alias("curr"),
        "product_name",
        "left"
    ) \
    .select(
        col("new.product_name"),
        col("new.category").alias("new_category"),
        col("curr.category").alias("old_category"),
        col("curr.product_key"),
        when(col("curr.product_key").isNull(), "INSERT")
        .when(col("new.category") != col("curr.category"), "UPDATE")
        .otherwise("NO_CHANGE").alias("change_type")
    )

print("\nDetected Changes:")
changes.show()

# Process SCD Type 2 updates
# 1. Expire old records
expired_records = current_dimension.alias("curr") \
    .join(
        changes.filter(col("change_type") == "UPDATE").alias("chg"),
        col("curr.product_name") == col("chg.product_name")
    ) \
    .select(
        col("curr.product_key"),
        col("curr.product_name"),
        col("curr.category"),
        col("curr.effective_date"),
        current_date().alias("end_date"),
        lit(False).alias("is_current")
    )

print("\nExpired Records:")
expired_records.show()

# 2. Create new records for updates
new_versions = changes.filter(col("change_type") == "UPDATE") \
    .select(
        (F.max(col("product_key")).over(Window.partitionBy()) + 1).alias("product_key"),
        "product_name",
        col("new_category").alias("category"),
        current_date().alias("effective_date"),
        lit("9999-12-31").cast("date").alias("end_date"),
        lit(True).alias("is_current")
    )

print("\nNew Versions for Updated Records:")
new_versions.show()

# 3. Insert new products
inserts = changes.filter(col("change_type") == "INSERT") \
    .select(
        (F.max(col("product_key")).over(Window.partitionBy()) + 2).alias("product_key"),
        "product_name",
        col("new_category").alias("category"),
        current_date().alias("effective_date"),
        lit("9999-12-31").cast("date").alias("end_date"),
        lit(True).alias("is_current")
    )

print("\nNew Product Inserts:")
inserts.show()

# 4. Combine all to create updated dimension
unchanged_records = current_dimension.alias("curr") \
    .join(
        changes.filter(col("change_type") != "NO_CHANGE").alias("chg"),
        col("curr.product_name") == col("chg.product_name"),
        "left_anti"
    )

updated_dimension = unchanged_records \
    .union(expired_records) \
    .union(new_versions) \
    .union(inserts)

print("\nUpdated Dimension (SCD Type 2):")
updated_dimension.orderBy("product_name", "effective_date").show()

# Create running totals, rankings, and other window-based transformations
window_data = spark.createDataFrame([
    ("2024-01", "Product_A", 100),
    ("2024-02", "Product_A", 150),
    ("2024-03", "Product_A", 120),
    ("2024-01", "Product_B", 80),
    ("2024-02", "Product_B", 90),
    ("2024-03", "Product_B", 110)
], ["month", "product", "sales"])

print("\nOriginal Data:")
window_data.show()

# Create various window-based metrics
from pyspark.sql.functions import rank, dense_rank, percent_rank, ntile

window_by_product = Window.partitionBy("product").orderBy("month")
window_all = Window.orderBy("month", "product")

windowed_metrics = window_data \
    .withColumn("running_total", _sum("sales").over(window_by_product)) \
    .withColumn("moving_avg_2", avg("sales").over(window_by_product.rowsBetween(-1, 0))) \
    .withColumn("prev_month_sales", F.lag("sales", 1).over(window_by_product)) \
    .withColumn("next_month_sales", F.lead("sales", 1).over(window_by_product)) \
    .withColumn("sales_change", col("sales") - F.lag("sales", 1).over(window_by_product)) \
    .withColumn("sales_rank", rank().over(Window.partitionBy("month").orderBy(col("sales").desc()))) \
    .withColumn("percentile", ntile(4).over(window_by_product))

print("\nWindow Function Metrics:")
windowed_metrics.show()

# Reshape window metrics to wide format for comparison
window_wide = windowed_metrics.groupBy("product") \
    .pivot("month") \
    .agg(first("sales").alias("sales"), first("running_total").alias("running_total"))

print("\nWindow Metrics in Wide Format:")
window_wide.show()

from pyspark.sql.functions import collect_list, concat_ws

# Normalized tables
employees = spark.createDataFrame([
    (1, "John"), (2, "Jane")
], ["emp_id", "name"])

    (1, "555-1234"), (1, "555-5678"), (2, "555-9012")
], ["emp_id", "phone"])

    phones.groupBy("emp_id").agg(

COMMON ISSUES AND SOLUTIONS:

1. PIVOT TOO SLOW
   Problem: Pivot operation taking too long
   Solutions:
   ✓ Specify pivot values explicitly
   ✓ Reduce cardinality by filtering or aggregating first
   ✓ Check if you really need pivot (consider alternatives)
   ✓ Increase executor memory
   
   # Bad
   df.groupBy("id").pivot("category").sum("value")
   
   # Good
   categories = ["cat1", "cat2", "cat3"]
   df.groupBy("id").pivot("category", categories).sum("value")

2. OUT OF MEMORY ERRORS
   Problem: Executor or driver running out of memory
   Solutions:
   ✓ Reduce number of pivot columns
   ✓ Use appropriate partitioning
   ✓ Avoid collect() on large datasets
   ✓ Use persist() instead of cache() with appropriate storage level
   ✓ Increase executor memory
   
   # Avoid
   large_df.collect()
   
   # Use
   large_df.write.parquet("output_path")

3. NULL VALUES AFTER PIVOT
   Problem: Unexpected nulls in pivoted columns
   Solutions:
   ✓ Use fillna() or coalesce()
   ✓ Check source data for nulls
   ✓ Use appropriate aggregation function
   
   # Handle nulls
   pivoted_df.fillna(0)
   # Or
   pivoted_df.na.fill({"col1": 0, "col2": "N/A"})

4. DUPLICATE ROWS AFTER UNPIVOT
   Problem: More rows than expected after unpivoting
   Solutions:
   ✓ Check for duplicate keys in source data
   ✓ Use distinct() if appropriate
   ✓ Validate source data quality
   
   # Check duplicates
   df.groupBy("key").count().filter(col("count") > 1).show()

5. DATA TYPE ISSUES
   Problem: Incorrect data types after reshaping
   Solutions:
   ✓ Cast explicitly
   ✓ Check schema after transformation
   ✓ Use appropriate aggregation functions
   
   # Explicit casting
   df.withColumn("value", col("value").cast("integer"))

6. PERFORMANCE DEGRADATION WITH COLLECT_LIST
   Problem: Slow performance with collect_list on large groups
   Solutions:
   ✓ Filter data before aggregation
   ✓ Use appropriate partitioning
   ✓ Consider if you really need all items in a list
   ✓ Set spark.sql.shuffle.partitions appropriately
   
   # Optimize
   spark.conf.set("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "200")

7. SKEWED DATA IN GROUP BY
   Problem: Some partitions much larger than others
   Solutions:
   ✓ Use salting technique
   ✓ Enable adaptive query execution
   ✓ Use appropriate partitioning keys
   
   # Enable AQE
   spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "true")
   spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled", "true")

8. STACK OVERFLOW WITH RECURSIVE OPERATIONS
   Problem: Too many iterations in hierarchy flattening
   Solutions:
   ✓ Limit recursion depth
   ✓ Use iterative approach with loop limit
   ✓ Consider GraphFrames for complex hierarchies
   
   # Set maximum iterations
   max_depth = 10
   for i in range(max_depth):
       # Your recursive logic
       if termination_condition:
           break
"""

COMMON FUNCTIONS:
─────────────────
• stack()           - Unpivot columns to rows
• pivot()           - Pivot rows to columns
• explode()         - Explode array to rows
• collect_list()    - Aggregate rows to array
• struct()          - Create nested structure
• array()           - Create array from columns
• map_from_arrays() - Create map from arrays
• concat_ws()       - Concatenate with separator

from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

def timing_decorator(func):
    """Decorator to measure function execution time"""
    @wraps(func)
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        start_time = time.time()
        result = func(*args, **kwargs)
        end_time = time.time()
        logger.info(f"{func.__name__} executed in {end_time - start_time:.2f} seconds")
        return result
    return wrapper

class LockContentionPattern:
    """
    Demonstrates lock contention issues when multiple tasks compete for shared resources.
    Common in scenarios with concurrent writes to the same partition or file.
    """
    
    def __init__(self, spark: SparkSession):
        self.spark = spark
        
    @timing_decorator
    def demonstrate_lock_contention_problem(self):
        """
        Problem: Multiple tasks trying to write to same partition simultaneously
        causing lock contention and performance degradation.
        """
        logger.info("=== Demonstrating Lock Contention Problem ===")
        
        # Create sample data with skewed partitioning
        data = [(i, i % 5, f"value_{i}") for i in range(10000)]
        df = self.spark.createDataFrame(data, ["id", "partition_key", "value"])
        
        # BAD: Writing with very few partitions causes lock contention
        # Multiple tasks compete for the same partition locks
        output_path = "/tmp/lock_contention_bad"
        
        start_time = time.time()
        df.repartition(2, "partition_key") \
          .write \
          .mode("overwrite") \
          .partitionBy("partition_key") \
          .parquet(output_path)
        
        logger.info(f"Lock contention write took: {time.time() - start_time:.2f}s")
        
    @timing_decorator
    def demonstrate_lock_contention_solution(self):
        """
        Solution: Optimize partitioning strategy to reduce lock contention
        """
        logger.info("=== Demonstrating Lock Contention Solution ===")
        
        # Create sample data
        data = [(i, i % 5, f"value_{i}") for i in range(10000)]
        df = self.spark.createDataFrame(data, ["id", "partition_key", "value"])
        
        # GOOD: Better partitioning strategy
        output_path = "/tmp/lock_contention_good"
        
        start_time = time.time()
        
        # Solution 1: Increase parallelism with appropriate partition count
        optimal_partitions = self.spark.sparkContext.defaultParallelism * 2
        
        df.repartition(optimal_partitions, "partition_key") \
          .write \
          .mode("overwrite") \
          .option("maxRecordsPerFile", 10000) \
          .partitionBy("partition_key") \
          .parquet(output_path)
        
        logger.info(f"Optimized write took: {time.time() - start_time:.2f}s")
        
    def demonstrate_broadcast_to_avoid_locks(self):
        """
        Solution: Use broadcast joins to avoid shuffle-based locks
        """
        logger.info("=== Using Broadcast to Avoid Lock Contention ===")
        
        # Large dataset
        large_data = [(i, f"large_{i}") for i in range(100000)]
        large_df = self.spark.createDataFrame(large_data, ["id", "large_value"])
        
        # Small lookup dataset
        small_data = [(i, f"small_{i}") for i in range(100)]
        small_df = self.spark.createDataFrame(small_data, ["id", "small_value"])
        
        # GOOD: Broadcast small table to avoid shuffle locks
        result = large_df.join(
            broadcast(small_df),
            "id",
            "left"
        )
        
        logger.info(f"Broadcast join result count: {result.count()}")

class MemoryContentionPattern:
    """
    Demonstrates memory contention when multiple tasks compete for limited memory,
    causing excessive GC, spilling to disk, or OOM errors.
    """
    
    def __init__(self, spark: SparkSession):
        self.spark = spark
        
    @timing_decorator
    def demonstrate_memory_contention_problem(self):
        """
        Problem: Memory-intensive operations causing contention and spilling
        """
        logger.info("=== Demonstrating Memory Contention Problem ===")
        
        # Create large dataset
        large_data = [(i, f"data_{i}" * 100, random.random()) 
                      for i in range(1000000)]
        df = self.spark.createDataFrame(large_data, ["id", "text", "value"])
        
        # BAD: Multiple memory-intensive operations without proper memory management
        # This can cause memory contention and spilling
        result = df \
            .groupBy("id") \
            .agg(
                collect_list("text").alias("texts"),  # Memory intensive
                collect_list("value").alias("values"),  # Memory intensive
                count("*").alias("count")
            ) \
            .cache()  # Caching large result adds to memory pressure
        
        logger.info(f"Memory contention result count: {result.count()}")
        result.unpersist()
        
    @timing_decorator
    def demonstrate_memory_contention_solution(self):
        """
        Solution: Optimize memory usage with proper configurations and techniques
        """
        logger.info("=== Demonstrating Memory Contention Solution ===")
        
        # Create large dataset
        large_data = [(i, f"data_{i}" * 100, random.random()) 
                      for i in range(1000000)]
        df = self.spark.createDataFrame(large_data, ["id", "text", "value"])
        
        # GOOD: Memory-optimized approach
        
        # Solution 1: Use aggregations that don't collect all data
        result = df \
            .groupBy("id") \
            .agg(
                count("*").alias("count"),
                sum("value").alias("sum_value"),
                avg("value").alias("avg_value")
            )
        
        # Solution 2: Partition data appropriately to distribute memory load
        result = result.repartition(
            self.spark.sparkContext.defaultParallelism * 3
        )
        
        # Solution 3: Use MEMORY_AND_DISK storage level for selective caching
        from pyspark import StorageLevel
        result.persist(StorageLevel.MEMORY_AND_DISK)
        
        logger.info(f"Optimized result count: {result.count()}")
        result.unpersist()
        
    def demonstrate_memory_efficient_window_operations(self):
        """
        Solution: Memory-efficient window operations
        """
        logger.info("=== Memory-Efficient Window Operations ===")
        
        # Create time-series data
        data = [(i, datetime.now() + timedelta(minutes=i), random.random()) 
                for i in range(100000)]
        df = self.spark.createDataFrame(data, ["id", "timestamp", "value"])
        
        # GOOD: Use rowsBetween instead of rangeBetween for better memory efficiency
        window_spec = Window \
            .orderBy("timestamp") \
            .rowsBetween(-100, 0)  # Limited window size
        
        result = df.withColumn(
            "rolling_avg",
            avg("value").over(window_spec)
        )
        
        logger.info(f"Window operation result count: {result.count()}")

class CPUContentionPattern:
    """
    Demonstrates CPU contention when tasks compete for CPU resources,
    causing increased processing time and reduced throughput.
    """
    
    def __init__(self, spark: SparkSession):
        self.spark = spark
        
    @timing_decorator
    def demonstrate_cpu_contention_problem(self):
        """
        Problem: CPU-intensive operations without proper parallelization
        """
        logger.info("=== Demonstrating CPU Contention Problem ===")
        
        # Create dataset for CPU-intensive processing
        data = [(i, f"text_{i}" * 1000) for i in range(10000)]
        df = self.spark.createDataFrame(data, ["id", "text"])
        
        # BAD: CPU-intensive UDF without proper parallelization
        def cpu_intensive_function(text):
            """Simulates CPU-intensive operation"""
            result = text
            for _ in range(100):
                result = result.upper().lower()
            return len(result)
        
        cpu_udf = udf(cpu_intensive_function, IntegerType())
        
        # Too few partitions cause CPU contention on fewer cores
        result = df.repartition(2).withColumn("processed", cpu_udf(col("text")))
        
        logger.info(f"CPU contention result count: {result.count()}")
        
    @timing_decorator
    def demonstrate_cpu_contention_solution(self):
        """
        Solution: Optimize CPU usage with proper parallelization
        """
        logger.info("=== Demonstrating CPU Contention Solution ===")
        
        # Create dataset
        data = [(i, f"text_{i}" * 1000) for i in range(10000)]
        df = self.spark.createDataFrame(data, ["id", "text"])
        
        # GOOD: Optimize parallelization for CPU-intensive operations
        
        # Solution 1: Use appropriate number of partitions
        optimal_partitions = self.spark.sparkContext.defaultParallelism * 2
        
        # Solution 2: Use Pandas UDF for better CPU utilization
        from pyspark.sql.functions import pandas_udf
        import pandas as pd
        
        @pandas_udf(IntegerType())
        def cpu_intensive_pandas_udf(texts: pd.Series) -> pd.Series:
            """Vectorized CPU-intensive operation"""
            def process_text(text):
                result = text
                for _ in range(100):
                    result = result.upper().lower()
                return len(result)
            
            return texts.apply(process_text)
        
        result = df \
            .repartition(optimal_partitions) \
            .withColumn("processed", cpu_intensive_pandas_udf(col("text")))
        
        logger.info(f"Optimized CPU result count: {result.count()}")
        
    def demonstrate_cpu_efficient_aggregations(self):
        """
        Solution: Use built-in aggregations instead of UDFs for better CPU efficiency
        """
        logger.info("=== CPU-Efficient Aggregations ===")
        
        # Create dataset
        data = [(i % 100, i, random.random()) for i in range(100000)]
        df = self.spark.createDataFrame(data, ["group_id", "id", "value"])
        
        # GOOD: Use built-in functions (optimized in native code)
        result = df.groupBy("group_id").agg(
            count("*").alias("count"),
            sum("value").alias("sum"),
            avg("value").alias("avg"),
            stddev("value").alias("stddev"),
            min("value").alias("min"),
            max("value").alias("max")
        )
        
        logger.info(f"CPU-efficient aggregation count: {result.count()}")

class NetworkContentionPattern:
    """
    Demonstrates network contention when data shuffling and transfer
    between nodes causes network bandwidth saturation.
    """
    
    def __init__(self, spark: SparkSession):
        self.spark = spark
        
    @timing_decorator
    def demonstrate_network_contention_problem(self):
        """
        Problem: Excessive data shuffling causing network contention
        """
        logger.info("=== Demonstrating Network Contention Problem ===")
        
        # Create large datasets
        data1 = [(i, f"value1_{i}", random.random()) for i in range(100000)]
        data2 = [(i % 50000, f"value2_{i}", random.random()) for i in range(100000)]
        
        df1 = self.spark.createDataFrame(data1, ["id", "value1", "metric1"])
        df2 = self.spark.createDataFrame(data2, ["id", "value2", "metric2"])
        
        # BAD: Multiple shuffles causing network contention
        
        # First shuffle - join
        joined = df1.join(df2, "id", "inner")
        
        # Second shuffle - repartition
        repartitioned = joined.repartition(200, "id")
        
        # Third shuffle - groupBy
        result = repartitioned.groupBy("id").agg(
            count("*").alias("count"),
            sum("metric1").alias("sum1"),
            sum("metric2").alias("sum2")
        )
        
        # Fourth shuffle - orderBy
        final_result = result.orderBy(desc("count"))
        
        logger.info(f"Network contention result count: {final_result.count()}")
        
    @timing_decorator
    def demonstrate_network_contention_solution(self):
        """
        Solution: Minimize shuffles and optimize data transfer
        """
        logger.info("=== Demonstrating Network Contention Solution ===")
        
        # Create datasets
        data1 = [(i, f"value1_{i}", random.random()) for i in range(100000)]
        data2 = [(i % 50000, f"value2_{i}", random.random()) for i in range(100000)]
        
        df1 = self.spark.createDataFrame(data1, ["id", "value1", "metric1"])
        df2 = self.spark.createDataFrame(data2, ["id", "value2", "metric2"])
        
        # GOOD: Minimize shuffles
        
        # Solution 1: Use broadcast join for smaller dataset
        joined = df1.join(broadcast(df2), "id", "inner")
        
        # Solution 2: Combine operations to reduce shuffles
        result = joined.groupBy("id").agg(
            count("*").alias("count"),
            sum("metric1").alias("sum1"),
            sum("metric2").alias("sum2")
        )
        
        # Solution 3: Use limit instead of full orderBy if possible
        final_result = result.orderBy(desc("count")).limit(1000)
        
        logger.info(f"Optimized network result count: {final_result.count()}")
        
    def demonstrate_partition_aware_joins(self):
        """
        Solution: Use partition-aware joins to reduce network transfer
        """
        logger.info("=== Partition-Aware Joins ===")
        
        # Create pre-partitioned datasets
        data1 = [(i, i % 100, f"value1_{i}") for i in range(100000)]
        data2 = [(i, i % 100, f"value2_{i}") for i in range(100000)]
        
        df1 = self.spark.createDataFrame(data1, ["id", "partition_key", "value1"])
        df2 = self.spark.createDataFrame(data2, ["id", "partition_key", "value2"])
        
        # GOOD: Pre-partition both datasets on the same key
        df1_partitioned = df1.repartition(50, "partition_key")
        df2_partitioned = df2.repartition(50, "partition_key")
        
        # Join on the partition key - reduces shuffle
        result = df1_partitioned.join(
            df2_partitioned,
            ["partition_key", "id"],
            "inner"
        )
        
        logger.info(f"Partition-aware join count: {result.count()}")
        
    def demonstrate_data_locality_optimization(self):
        """
        Solution: Optimize data locality to reduce network transfer
        """
        logger.info("=== Data Locality Optimization ===")
        
        # Create dataset
        data = [(i, i % 10, f"value_{i}", random.random()) 
                for i in range(100000)]
        df = self.spark.createDataFrame(
            data, 
            ["id", "group_id", "value", "metric"]
        )
        
        # GOOD: Cache frequently accessed data to improve locality
        df.cache()
        
        # Perform multiple operations on cached data (no network transfer)
        result1 = df.groupBy("group_id").agg(count("*").alias("count"))
        result2 = df.groupBy("group_id").agg(avg("metric").alias("avg_metric"))
        result3 = df.groupBy("group_id").agg(sum("metric").alias("sum_metric"))
        
        logger.info(f"Locality optimized results: {result1.count()}, "
                   f"{result2.count()}, {result3.count()}")
        
        df.unpersist()
        
    def demonstrate_skew_handling_for_network(self):
        """
        Solution: Handle data skew to prevent network hotspots
        """
        logger.info("=== Handling Data Skew for Network Optimization ===")
        
        # Create skewed dataset (most records have same key)
        skewed_data = [(1 if i < 80000 else i % 100, f"value_{i}", random.random()) 
                       for i in range(100000)]
        df = self.spark.createDataFrame(skewed_data, ["key", "value", "metric"])
        
        # BAD: Direct groupBy on skewed key causes network hotspot
        # One partition receives most data
        
        # GOOD: Add salt to distribute skewed keys
        from pyspark.sql.functions import rand, floor
        
        # Add random salt
        salted_df = df.withColumn("salt", floor(rand() * 10))
        
        # Create salted key
        salted_df = salted_df.withColumn(
            "salted_key",
            concat(col("key").cast("string"), lit("_"), col("salt").cast("string"))
        )
        
        # Group by salted key
        intermediate_result = salted_df.groupBy("salted_key", "key").agg(
            count("*").alias("count"),
            sum("metric").alias("sum_metric")
        )
        
        # Final aggregation
        final_result = intermediate_result.groupBy("key").agg(
            sum("count").alias("total_count"),
            sum("sum_metric").alias("total_sum")
        )
        
        logger.info(f"Skew-handled result count: {final_result.count()}")

class ResourceContentionMonitor:
    """
    Utility class to monitor and report on resource contention issues
    """
    
    def __init__(self, spark: SparkSession):
        self.spark = spark
        
    def check_partition_distribution(self, df, partition_col=None):
        """
        Check if data is evenly distributed across partitions
        """
        logger.info("=== Checking Partition Distribution ===")
        
        if partition_col:
            # Check distribution by partition column
            distribution = df.groupBy(partition_col).count()
            stats = distribution.agg(
                min("count").alias("min_count"),
                max("count").alias("max_count"),
                avg("count").alias("avg_count"),
                stddev("count").alias("stddev_count")
            ).collect()[0]
            
            logger.info(f"Partition distribution stats:")
            logger.info(f"  Min: {stats['min_count']}")
            logger.info(f"  Max: {stats['max_count']}")
            logger.info(f"  Avg: {stats['avg_count']:.2f}")
            logger.info(f"  StdDev: {stats['stddev_count']:.2f}")
            
            # Check for skew
            skew_ratio = stats['max_count'] / stats['avg_count']
            if skew_ratio > 2.0:
                logger.warning(f"Data skew detected! Skew ratio: {skew_ratio:.2f}")
            else:
                logger.info(f"Partition distribution is balanced. Skew ratio: {skew_ratio:.2f}")
        
        # Check physical partitions
        num_partitions = df.rdd.getNumPartitions()
        logger.info(f"Number of physical partitions: {num_partitions}")
        
        return num_partitions
        
    def get_optimal_partition_count(self, df, target_partition_size_mb=128):
        """
        Calculate optimal partition count based on data size
        """
        # Estimate data size (this is approximate)
        sample_size = df.limit(1000).count()
        if sample_size > 0:
            total_count = df.count()
            
            # Rough estimation
            optimal_partitions = max(
                self.spark.sparkContext.defaultParallelism,
                int(total_count / 10000)  # Rough heuristic
            )
            
            logger.info(f"Recommended partition count: {optimal_partitions}")
            return optimal_partitions
        
        return self.spark.sparkContext.defaultParallelism
        
    def analyze_shuffle_operations(self, df):
        """
        Analyze potential shuffle operations in query plan
        """
        logger.info("=== Analyzing Shuffle Operations ===")
        
        # Get the physical plan
        plan = df._jdf.queryExecution().executedPlan().toString()
        
        # Count shuffle operations
        shuffle_count = plan.count("Exchange")
        sort_count = plan.count("Sort")
        
        logger.info(f"Detected shuffle operations: {shuffle_count}")
        logger.info(f"Detected sort operations: {sort_count}")
        
        if shuffle_count > 3:
            logger.warning("High number of shuffles detected! Consider optimization.")
            
        return shuffle_count
        
    def recommend_configurations(self, workload_type="balanced"):
        """
        Recommend Spark configurations based on workload type
        """
        logger.info(f"=== Configuration Recommendations for {workload_type} workload ===")
        
        configs = {}
        
        if workload_type == "memory_intensive":

            }
        elif workload_type == "cpu_intensive":
            configs = {
                "spark.executor.cores": "4",
                "spark.task.cpus": "1",

            }
        elif workload_type == "io_intensive":

                "spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes": "134217728",  # 128MB

                "spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled": "true"
            }
        elif workload_type == "network_intensive":

class ContentionMitigationStrategies:
    """
    Additional strategies and utilities for mitigating resource contention
    """
    
    @staticmethod
    def adaptive_repartitioning(df, spark, target_size_mb=128):
        """
        Adaptively repartition based on data size
        """
        # Get current partition count
        current_partitions = df.rdd.getNumPartitions()
        
        # Calculate optimal partitions
        # This is a simplified calculation
        optimal_partitions = max(
            spark.sparkContext.defaultParallelism,
            current_partitions
        )
        
        logger.info(f"Repartitioning from {current_partitions} to {optimal_partitions}")
        
        return df.repartition(optimal_partitions)
    
    @staticmethod
    def smart_cache_strategy(df, cache_level="MEMORY_AND_DISK"):
        """
        Implement smart caching based on data size and access patterns
        """
        from pyspark import StorageLevel
        
        storage_levels = {
            "MEMORY_ONLY": StorageLevel.MEMORY_ONLY,
            "MEMORY_AND_DISK": StorageLevel.MEMORY_AND_DISK,
            "MEMORY_AND_DISK_SER": StorageLevel.MEMORY_AND_DISK_SER,
            "DISK_ONLY": StorageLevel.DISK_ONLY
        }
        
        level = storage_levels.get(cache_level, StorageLevel.MEMORY_AND_DISK)
        
        logger.info(f"Caching with storage level: {cache_level}")
        return df.persist(level)
    
    @staticmethod
    def optimize_join_strategy(df1, df2, join_key, join_type="inner", 
                               broadcast_threshold_mb=10):
        """
        Automatically choose optimal join strategy
        """
        # Try to estimate data sizes (simplified)
        df2_sample_count = df2.limit(10000).count()
        
        # If right side is small, use broadcast join
        if df2_sample_count < broadcast_threshold_mb * 10000:
            logger.info("Using broadcast join strategy")
            return df1.join(broadcast(df2), join_key, join_type)
        else:
            logger.info("Using sort-merge join strategy")
            # Pre-partition both sides
            df1_partitioned = df1.repartition(200, join_key)
            df2_partitioned = df2.repartition(200, join_key)
            return df1_partitioned.join(df2_partitioned, join_key, join_type)
    
    @staticmethod
    def handle_data_skew_with_salting(df, skewed_column, num_salts=10):
        """
        Handle data skew using salting technique
        """
        logger.info(f"Applying salting to {skewed_column} with {num_salts} salts")
        
        # Add salt column
        salted_df = df.withColumn(
            "salt",
            (rand() * num_salts).cast("int")
        )
        
        # Create composite key
        salted_df = salted_df.withColumn(
            f"{skewed_column}_salted",
            concat(
                col(skewed_column).cast("string"),
                lit("_"),
                col("salt").cast("string")
            )
        )
        
        return salted_df
    
    @staticmethod
    def optimize_file_output(df, output_path, target_file_size_mb=128, 
                            compression="snappy"):
        """
        Optimize file output to reduce I/O contention
        """
        # Calculate records per file based on target size
        max_records_per_file = target_file_size_mb * 10000  # Rough estimate
        
        logger.info(f"Writing with target file size: {target_file_size_mb}MB")
        logger.info(f"Max records per file: {max_records_per_file}")
        
        df.write \
          .mode("overwrite") \
          .option("maxRecordsPerFile", max_records_per_file) \
          .option("compression", compression) \
          .parquet(output_path)
        
        logger.info(f"Data written to {output_path}")

# ============================================================================

class PerformanceComparator:
    """
    Utility to compare performance of different approaches
    """
    
    def __init__(self, spark):
        self.spark = spark
        self.results = []
    
    def benchmark_operation(self, name, operation_func, *args, **kwargs):
        """
        Benchmark a specific operation
        """
        logger.info(f"\nBenchmarking: {name}")
        
        start_time = time.time()
        try:
            result = operation_func(*args, **kwargs)
            
            # Force evaluation if it's a DataFrame
            if hasattr(result, 'count'):
                count = result.count()
            else:
                count = "N/A"
            
            end_time = time.time()
            duration = end_time - start_time
            
            self.results.append({
                'name': name,
                'duration': duration,
                'count': count,
                'status': 'SUCCESS'
            })
            
            logger.info(f"  Duration: {duration:.2f}s")
            logger.info(f"  Result count: {count}")
            
            return result
            
        except Exception as e:
            end_time = time.time()
            duration = end_time - start_time
            
            self.results.append({
                'name': name,
                'duration': duration,
                'count': 0,
                'status': 'FAILED',
                'error': str(e)
            })
            
            logger.error(f"  Failed after {duration:.2f}s: {str(e)}")
            raise
    
    def print_summary(self):
        """
        Print performance comparison summary
        """
        logger.info("\n" + "=" * 80)
        logger.info("PERFORMANCE COMPARISON SUMMARY")
        logger.info("=" * 80)
        
        for result in self.results:
            logger.info(f"\n{result['name']}:")
            logger.info(f"  Status: {result['status']}")
            logger.info(f"  Duration: {result['duration']:.2f}s")
            logger.info(f"  Count: {result['count']}")
            if 'error' in result:
                logger.info(f"  Error: {result['error']}")
        
        # Find fastest and slowest
        successful_results = [r for r in self.results if r['status'] == 'SUCCESS']
        if successful_results:
            fastest = min(successful_results, key=lambda x: x['duration'])
            slowest = max(successful_results, key=lambda x: x['duration'])
            
            logger.info("\n" + "-" * 80)
            logger.info(f"Fastest: {fastest['name']} ({fastest['duration']:.2f}s)")
            logger.info(f"Slowest: {slowest['name']} ({slowest['duration']:.2f}s)")
            
            if slowest['duration'] > 0:
                speedup = slowest['duration'] / fastest['duration']
                logger.info(f"Speedup: {speedup:.2f}x")

def example_real_world_scenarios(spark):
    """
    Demonstrate real-world scenarios with resource contention
    """
    logger.info("\n" + "=" * 80)
    logger.info("REAL-WORLD SCENARIO EXAMPLES")
    logger.info("=" * 80)
    
    comparator = PerformanceComparator(spark)
    strategies = ContentionMitigationStrategies()
    
    # Scenario 1: Large-scale ETL with multiple joins
    logger.info("\n--- Scenario 1: Large-scale ETL Pipeline ---")
    
    # Create sample datasets
    customers = spark.createDataFrame(
        [(i, f"customer_{i}", i % 100) for i in range(100000)],
        ["customer_id", "name", "region_id"]
    )
    
    orders = spark.createDataFrame(
        [(i, i % 100000, random.random() * 1000) for i in range(500000)],
        ["order_id", "customer_id", "amount"]
    )
    
    regions = spark.createDataFrame(
        [(i, f"region_{i}") for i in range(100)],
        ["region_id", "region_name"]
    )
    
    # Bad approach - multiple shuffles
    def etl_with_contention():
        result = orders \
            .join(customers, "customer_id") \
            .join(regions, "region_id") \
            .groupBy("region_name") \
            .agg(
                count("*").alias("order_count"),
                sum("amount").alias("total_amount")
            ) \
            .orderBy(desc("total_amount"))
        return result
    
    # Good approach - optimized
    def etl_optimized():
        # Broadcast small tables
        result = orders \
            .join(broadcast(customers), "customer_id") \
            .join(broadcast(regions), "region_id") \
            .groupBy("region_name") \
            .agg(
                count("*").alias("order_count"),
                sum("amount").alias("total_amount")
            ) \
            .orderBy(desc("total_amount"))
        return result
    
    comparator.benchmark_operation(
        "ETL with Contention",
        etl_with_contention
    )
    
    comparator.benchmark_operation(
        "ETL Optimized",
        etl_optimized
    )
    
    # Scenario 2: Handling skewed data in aggregations
    logger.info("\n--- Scenario 2: Skewed Data Aggregation ---")
    
    # Create heavily skewed dataset
    skewed_data = []
    for i in range(100000):
        if i < 80000:
            key = "popular_key"
        else:
            key = f"key_{i % 1000}"
        skewed_data.append((key, random.random()))
    
    skewed_df = spark.createDataFrame(skewed_data, ["key", "value"])
    
    # Bad approach - direct aggregation
    def aggregate_skewed():
        return skewed_df.groupBy("key").agg(
            count("*").alias("count"),
            avg("value").alias("avg_value")
        )
    
    # Good approach - with salting
    def aggregate_with_salting():
        salted = strategies.handle_data_skew_with_salting(skewed_df, "key", 20)
        
        # Aggregate with salted key
        intermediate = salted.groupBy("key_salted", "key").agg(
            count("*").alias("count"),
            sum("value").alias("sum_value"),
            count("value").alias("count_value")
        )
        
        # Final aggregation
        final = intermediate.groupBy("key").agg(
            sum("count").alias("count"),
            (sum("sum_value") / sum("count_value")).alias("avg_value")
        )
        
        return final
    
    comparator.benchmark_operation(
        "Skewed Aggregation - No Optimization",
        aggregate_skewed
    )
    
    comparator.benchmark_operation(
        "Skewed Aggregation - With Salting",
        aggregate_with_salting
    )
    
    # Scenario 3: Memory-intensive window operations
    logger.info("\n--- Scenario 3: Window Operations ---")
    
    time_series = spark.createDataFrame(
        [(i, datetime.now() + timedelta(minutes=i), random.random()) 
         for i in range(50000)],
        ["id", "timestamp", "value"]
    )
    
    # Bad approach - unbounded window
    def window_unbounded():
```python
    def window_unbounded():
        window_spec = Window.orderBy("timestamp")
        return time_series.withColumn(
            "cumulative_sum",
            sum("value").over(window_spec)
        )
    
    # Good approach - bounded window
    def window_bounded():
        window_spec = Window.orderBy("timestamp").rowsBetween(-1000, 0)
        return time_series.withColumn(
            "rolling_sum",
            sum("value").over(window_spec)
        )
    
    comparator.benchmark_operation(
        "Window - Unbounded (Memory Intensive)",
        window_unbounded
    )
    
    comparator.benchmark_operation(
        "Window - Bounded (Memory Efficient)",
        window_bounded
    )
    
    # Print comparison summary
    comparator.print_summary()
